FACTS.identity: Wang Jianhua, male，56 years old, married, from Chengdu。
FACTS.pain:
Record time：2026-09-01 10:00
Chief complaint：Recurrent abdominal distension for 6 months, worsening with lower-extremity edema for 10 days and decreased urine output for 2 days.
History of present illness：The Patient was found to be hepatitis B surface antigen-positive during a health examination 20 years ago and was diagnosed with hepatitis B-related cirrhosis by liver imaging and blood tests 3 years ago. Abdominal distension and bilateral lower-extremity edema first developed 6 months ago and improved with outpatient antiviral and oral diuretic treatment; there was no hospitalization or paracentesis. Abdominal girth has been essentially stable over the past month. On August 20, weight was 68 kg and creatinine was 78 μmol/L.
Abdominal distension gradually worsened after a group meal and increased consumption of preserved foods 10 days ago, with a tighter waistband, early satiety, and bilateral ankle edema extending to the lower legs. From August 28 to 30, the patient independently increased furosemide from 20 mg/day to 40 mg/day while continuing spironolactone at 50 mg/day, without significant relief of abdominal distension. Over the past 3 days, food intake has been approximately half the usual amount, with water intake of approximately 1000 mL/day. Over the past 2 days, estimated urine output decreased from approximately 1500 mL/day to 800–1000 mL/day, with dark urine and worsening fatigue after activity.
No chills; maximum self-measured temperature 37.4°C. Only mild, diffuse, dull abdominal pain, without persistent, localized severe pain. No vomiting, diarrhea, hematemesis, or melena; recent stools have been yellow-brown, once daily. No cough, sputum production, or dysuria; no sleep–wake reversal, abnormal behavior, or confusion. Able to lie flat at night, with no chest pain or orthopnea. Marked ascites and relatively low blood pressure were noted at today’s outpatient visit, prompting admission.
Recent medication use and exposures：Regularly takes entecavir 1 mg/day (previous decompensation), spironolactone 50 mg/day, and furosemide 20 mg/day; had not yet taken diuretics on the day of admission. Denies recent NSAIDs, Chinese herbal medicines, contrast agents, or other nephrotoxic drugs. No hospitalization or antibiotic use in the past 3 months, and no known history of colonization with resistant organisms.
Since onset, slightly reduced energy, sleep affected by abdominal distension, and decreased appetite. Recent weight gain is primarily attributed to fluid retention; weight gain does not exclude nutritional risk.
FACTS.past:
History of liver disease：Hepatitis B for approximately 20 years; follow-up was irregular initially. Started entecavir 1 mg once daily on an empty stomach after developing ascites 6 months ago; denies missed doses or prior use of nucleoside analogues such as lamivudine. No prior SBP, hepatic encephalopathy, gastrointestinal bleeding, liver cancer, or portal vein thrombosis.
Previous examinations：2026-06-15 outpatient gastroscopy summary: small varices in the lower esophagus, without red signs or active bleeding; mild portal hypertensive gastropathy. A nonselective beta-blocker has not yet been started because outpatient systolic blood pressure is usually 95–100 mmHg, with occasional dizziness; hepatology reassessment is planned. On 2026-08-20, creatinine was 78 μmol/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, and potassium 4.2 mmol/L; there was no significant edema at that time, and weight was 68 kg. The above is a summary of historical records; no original gastroscopy images have been fabricated.
Other past medical history：Denies a history of hypertension, diabetes, coronary artery disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, tuberculosis, or malignancy. No history of surgery, trauma, or transfusion. Vaccination details are unknown. Denies known food or drug allergies.
Personal history：Born in and a long-term resident of Chengdu, Sichuan; married, lives with his wife, and has one son. Approximately 10 pack-years of smoking; quit 5 years ago. Previously drank small amounts of alcohol; stopped after diagnosis of cirrhosis. No intravenous drug use, tattoos, or recent exposure to contaminated water in endemic areas. Work mainly involves standing and light manual handling.
Family history：Mother is hepatitis B surface antigen positive; no known history of liver cancer. Father has hypertension. No known hereditary liver or kidney disease.
Review of systems：No recent significant weight loss or night sweats; no chest tightness, palpitations, or unilateral lower-limb swelling and pain; no frequent small-volume urination, hematuria, or foamy urine; no rash or joint swelling and pain; no visual abnormalities or focal neurological symptoms.

sheet.title: Therapeutic Paracentesis Record
sheet.findings:
2026-09-04　Start 10:00，End 11:40
Preprocedural diagnosis and indications：Cirrhosis with large-volume ascites; good response to SBP treatment and recovery of renal function. Persistent marked abdominal distension and early satiety, with a tense abdominal wall. BP 108/68 mmHg, pulse 82/min, SpO2 98%. Currently does not meet the definition of refractory ascites.
Informed consent and preparation：The purpose of drainage, albumin replacement, and risks including bleeding, infection, hypotension, circulatory dysfunction, and leakage were explained; the Patient consented. Identity and the ultrasound window were verified, and the bladder was emptied; no prophylactic plasma or platelet transfusion.
Procedure details：The patient was placed in a semi-recumbent position. Ultrasound identified a safe fluid pocket in the left lower abdomen, avoiding abdominal wall vessels. Following routine sterile skin preparation and draping, local anesthesia with 5 mL of 1% lidocaine was administered, and a disposable paracentesis catheter was inserted. A total of 6000 mL of clear, pale-yellow ascitic fluid was drained slowly in stages with observation. Vital signs and symptoms were checked every 15 minutes. No catheter was left for continuous drainage. On completion, the catheter was removed, pressure applied, and a sterile dressing placed.
Albumin and safety records：Based on 6 L drained × 8 g/L, administer an additional 48 g (240 mL) of 20% human albumin by slow IV infusion after the procedure, with monitoring. This is indicated for paracentesis and is documented separately from the SBP regimens on 09-01 and 09-03, not counted twice on the same day.
Postoperative：Latest BP 106/66 mmHg, P 80 beats/min, SpO₂ 98%; abdominal distension markedly improved, abdominal girth decreased from 105 cm to 96 cm, and weight decreased from 75.6 kg to 69.6 kg. No local bleeding or fluid leakage, worsening abdominal pain, or syncope. Continue observation for 2 hours and recheck renal function and electrolytes the next morning.
Procedural physician: Zhao Heng; supervising physician: Shen Yan; nurse: Jiang Yue (all simulated roles). No surgical operation was performed in this case; this is an invasive procedure record.
